title: The Transitional Program for Socialist Revolution
author: Leon Trotsky (with contributions from the Fourth International)
target_audience: Historians and students of political science
core_themes: Transitional demands as a method for mobilizing the working class
The necessity of revolutionary leadership and a vanguard party
Analyzing capitalism in its imperialist and crisis phase
Preparation for socialist revolution through mass action
The inadequacy of minimum/reformist programs in a period of capitalist decay
primary_purpose: To outline a strategy for revolutionary socialist parties to bridge the immediate struggles and consciousness of the working class with the ultimate goal of socialist revolution, providing practical and ideological guidance through transitional demands that expose the limitations of capitalism and prepare the movement for the seizure of power.

structure_format.organization: Divided into short, focused sections that address the historical context, tactics (transitional demands), and organizational requirements for socialist revolution.
features: Systematic explanation of transitional vs. minimum/maximum programs
Detailed transitional demands (e.g., sliding scale of wages and hours, workers' control of production)
Analysis of capitalist crisis and the rise of fascism
Call for the building of new, revolutionary parties and the Fourth International

key_concepts_lessons: Transitional demands connect everyday struggles to revolutionary objectives, exposing capitalism’s limits.
A revolutionary party is essential; reformist and centrist organizations can’t lead the working class to victory.
Capitalism in crisis cannot offer lasting reforms—crises open revolutionary possibilities.
Broad, militant demands (unemployment, wage rises, workers’ control) accelerate class consciousness.
Only democratic, mass action and workers’ councils can counteract fascism and reaction.
The socialist revolution is a practical, not utopian, necessity in periods of capitalist decay.
notable_features: Introduces the concept of the 'Transitional Program' as a dynamic strategy rather than a static set of reforms
Focuses heavily on the need for an international revolutionary organization (the Fourth International)
Grounds every demand in concrete conditions of late-1930s capitalist crisis
Features a sharp critique of reformism, Stalinism, and traditional social-democracy
cultural_historical_context: Written in 1938 amid global economic depression, rising fascism, and the degeneration of the Soviet Union under Stalinism, the document served as the foundational program of the newly formed Fourth International, aiming to re-arm the workers' movement with revolutionary Marxist tactics after betrayals by social-democratic and Stalinist parties.
reception_impact: Enduring foundational document for Trotskyist organizations worldwide
Highly influential in shaping Marxist debates on revolutionary strategies post-World War II
Subject of debate and reinterpretation within the socialist left regarding relevance to later eras
Critiqued by some for rigidity or for relying on assumptions specific to the 1930s
comparable_titles: The Communist Manifesto by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels
What Is to Be Done? by V.I. Lenin
Left-Wing Communism: An Infantile Disorder by V.I. Lenin
The Revolution Betrayed by Leon Trotsky
